about.p: *Collocations* are the word partnerships that sound natural to native speakers: we say *heavy rain* and *make a decision*, not *strong rain* or *do a decision*. Learning words together with their usual partners makes your English sound natural and helps you say exactly what you mean.

Units 1–5 teach you how to find and record collocations and how they differ in register. Units 6–12 look at grammatical patterns (intensifying adverbs, everyday verbs) and special areas such as metaphor. The rest of the book presents collocations by topic and by function. Each **left-hand page** presents the collocations in texts and examples; the **right-hand page** practises them.

about.-: Learn each collocation as one unit: on every card the whole phrase is the item, with its meaning and an example.
*Complete the phrase* questions hide one word of the collocation and ask you to choose it: this is the book's main exercise, choosing the word that goes with another.
This course follows the second edition. Two first-edition units that are not in the second edition (Feelings and emotions, Computers) are added at the end.

about.tip: When you read in English, notice word partners and write them down as pairs: not *rain* but *heavy rain*, *torrential rain*, *the rain stopped*.

units.sub: strong coffee, pay attention, pitch dark

L.p: A *collocation* is a natural word partnership: two or more words that native speakers regularly put together. We say *strong coffee* and *heavy traffic*, not *powerful coffee* or *thick traffic*; we *pay attention* and *commit a crime*. Grammar does not explain these choices – they are simply the combinations that sound right to speakers of English.

L.e: I need a cup of strong coffee before work. There was heavy traffic on the ring road. Please pay attention to the safety instructions. The man admitted that he had committed the crime.

L.x: The motorway was full of *heavy traffic* (not *big traffic*) all morning.

L.p: Using the right partners makes your English sound natural, and listeners understand you immediately. Collocations also help you replace general words such as *very*, *nice*, *big* and *get* with more precise ones: instead of *a very big problem*, say *a serious problem* or *a major problem*; instead of *get a prize*, say *win a prize*.

L.e: The storm caused serious damage to the harbour. Unemployment remains a major concern. She won first prize in the photography competition. We had a long chat over coffee.

L.p: Some words combine with almost anything: a car can be *new*, *old*, *red* or *expensive*. Others have very few partners: you *shrug* your *shoulders* and nothing else, and *pitch* (meaning 'completely') goes with *dark* or *black*. These strong collocations are especially worth learning, because once you know one word, you know the other.

L.e: When I asked where the keys were, he just shrugged his shoulders. The power went off and the house was pitch dark. Did you catch a cold on the trip? If you make a promise, keep it.

units.sub: break the news, a close friend, keep a record

L.p: Collocations are everywhere in what you read and hear. Notice them in articles, songs, films and conversations, and look for words that keep appearing together: a *daily routine*, a *close friend*, *break the news*. Online, a corpus or a search engine can show you how common a combination is.

L.e: In today's news article I noticed *launch an investigation*, *a growing number of* and *public opinion*. In a podcast I heard *break the news* twice.

L.p: Record collocations in groups that make sense to you: by key word (*decision*: make, reach, take a decision; a tough, final, *hasty* decision), by topic (weather, work, travel), or in a word fork – a diagram with the key word in the middle and its partners around it. Always add a full example sentence and note anything unusual, such as a preposition.

L.e: decision → make / reach / take a decision; a tough / final / hasty decision. weather → heavy rain, strong wind, thick fog, bright sunshine.

L.tip: Write the whole phrase on one side of a card and a translation or picture on the other. Testing yourself in both directions works better than reading a list.

L.p: Review new collocations several times in the first few weeks – little and often works best. Use them in sentences about your own life and say them aloud until they feel automatic. When you look up a new word, look for its common partners as well as its meaning, and *keep a record of* them.

L.e: Every evening I spend ten minutes testing myself on the day's collocations. I wrote a diary entry using break the news, a close friend and reach a decision.

units.sub: undivided attention, heated argument, make an effort

L.h: A What a learner's dictionary tells you

L.p: A good learner's dictionary does more than explain meanings. It shows a word's typical partners in example sentences and often in special collocation boxes. For the noun *attention*, for example, it may list verbs (*attract*, *pay*, *draw* attention *to*), adjectives (*close*, *undivided*) and phrases (*the centre of attention*).

L.e: The entry for *argument* includes have an argument, win an argument, a heated argument and a convincing argument. The new restaurant has attracted a lot of attention.

L.p: A collocation dictionary is organised around key words and lists their common partners by type: adjectives, verbs, prepositions. An online corpus lets you type in a word and see thousands of real examples, so you can check which combination is more natural, for example *heavy rain* or *strong rain* (heavy rain, by far).

L.e: I searched a corpus and found make an effort hundreds of times more often than do an effort.

L.x: We should *make an effort* (not *do an effort*) to arrive early.

L.p: Read the example sentences: they often contain the most useful collocations. Notice labels such as *formal*, *informal* or *disapproving*, the prepositions a word takes (*interested in*, *responsible for*), and whether a noun is countable or uncountable.

L.e: The entry for *responsible* shows responsible for something and responsible to someone: Nurses are responsible for patient care and responsible to the ward manager.

units.sub: narrow escape, a round of applause, burst into tears

L.h: A Adjective + noun and noun + verb

L.p: Collocations come in several grammatical patterns. Adjectives often have favourite nouns: a *narrow escape*, a *rough guess*, a *sharp increase*, a *light meal*. Nouns also have favourite verbs that describe what they do: a storm *breaks*, a dog *barks*, prices *rise*, an engine *starts*.

L.e: The driver had a narrow escape when his car slid off the road. At a rough guess, about two hundred people came. There has been a sharp increase in rents this year. The storm broke just as we left the beach.

L.h: B Noun + noun and verb + noun

L.p: Some nouns combine in an *of* pattern: a *round of applause*, a *pang of guilt*, a *sense of pride*, a *bunch of flowers*. Verbs and their objects form many collocations: *run a business*, *keep a secret*, *set a record*, *hold a meeting*.

L.e: The speaker received a long round of applause. I felt a pang of guilt when I saw her sad face. My aunt runs a small business from home. Can you keep a secret? The athlete set a new world record.

L.h: C Verb + preposition phrase, verb + adverb, adverb + adjective

L.p: Some verbs combine with fixed prepositional phrases: *burst into tears*, *fall in love*, *run out of time*, *come to an end*. Verbs and adverbs pair up too: *rely heavily on*, *vaguely remember*, *smile proudly*. And adverbs often go with particular adjectives: *happily married*, *fully aware*, *deeply moved*.

L.e: When she heard the news, she burst into tears. We ran out of time before the last question. The town relies heavily on tourism. I vaguely remember meeting him. They've been happily married for forty years.

units.sub: pretty awful, submit an application, lodge an appeal

L.p: Some collocations belong to relaxed, spoken English. *Pretty* meaning 'fairly' is informal, especially with negative adjectives: *pretty awful*, *pretty bad*, *pretty boring*. Other informal combinations include *have a go* (try), *a bit of a mess*, *make a fuss* (complain or get excited about something unimportant) and *a load of rubbish* (nonsense).

L.e: The film was pretty awful, to be honest. Can I have a go on your skateboard? The kitchen's a bit of a mess. Don't make a fuss – it's only a scratch. What he said was a load of rubbish.

L.p: Official letters, notices and academic texts use more formal partnerships: *submit an application* (rather than *send* one), *commence proceedings* (start legal action), *express your gratitude* (say thank you), *be in receipt of* (have received).

L.e: Please submit your application by 1 May. We wish to express our gratitude for your support. We are in receipt of your letter of 12 March. The company has commenced legal proceedings.

L.x: In a formal letter, write *I am writing to express my gratitude* (not *I am writing to say a big thanks*).

L.p: Each profession has its own collocations. In law, you *lodge an appeal* and a jury *reaches a verdict*; in medicine, nurses *administer* a drug and doctors *carry out* tests; in business, customers *place an order* and companies *meet demand*.

L.e: Her lawyers will lodge an appeal against the sentence. The jury reached a verdict after two days. The nurse administered the injection. The factory can't meet demand at the moment.

units.sub: highly unlikely, utterly ridiculous, strongly object

L.p: Adverbs such as *very* can make English sound flat. Stronger adverbs have their own preferred partners: *highly* goes with *unlikely*, *successful*, *recommended* and *qualified*; *utterly* (completely) mostly with negative words like *ridiculous*, *exhausted* and *pointless*; *bitterly* with *cold* and *disappointed*; *deeply* with feelings such as *concerned*, *moved* and *hurt*; *seriously* with *ill* and *injured*; *perfectly* with *normal*, *clear* and *safe*.

L.e: It's highly unlikely that the plane will leave on time. The idea of charging for the park is utterly ridiculous. It was bitterly cold at the top of the mountain. I was deeply moved by her speech. Two passengers were seriously injured. It's perfectly normal to feel nervous before an exam.

L.x: I was *bitterly disappointed* (not *highly disappointed*) with the result.

L.p: Verbs also have typical intensifiers: you *strongly object to*, *strongly recommend* or *strongly believe* something; you *deeply regret* a mistake; you *sincerely hope* for a good outcome; you *fully understand* a problem; and you *flatly refuse* when you say no very firmly.

L.e: Many residents strongly object to the new road. I strongly recommend booking in advance. We deeply regret any inconvenience. I sincerely hope you feel better soon. She flatly refused to discuss the matter.

L.p: Some adjectives intensify nouns: *a complete waste of time*, *an utter disaster*, *a total stranger*, *a real pleasure*.

L.e: The meeting was a complete waste of time. The picnic was an utter disaster – it poured all afternoon. A total stranger helped me change my tyre.

units.sub: make a mistake, do your best, do damage

L.p: *Make* often goes with nouns for things we produce, cause or carry out: *make a mistake*, *make a decision*, *make an effort*, *make progress*, *make a noise*, *make a profit* or *a loss*, *make a difference* (have a good effect). It is also used for some things we say: *make a complaint*, *make a suggestion*, *make an excuse*, *make a promise*.

L.e: I made a silly mistake in the last question. The new teacher has really made a difference to the school. Our café made a small profit in its first year. Are you making progress with your driving lessons? He made an excuse and left early. Several guests made a complaint about the noise.

L.x: Everyone *makes mistakes* (not *does mistakes*) when they learn a language.

L.p: *Do* goes with tasks, jobs and general activities: *do the shopping*, *do the washing-up*, *do your homework*, *do research*, *do business*, *do someone a favour*. It also appears in fixed phrases about results: *do damage*, *do harm*, *do (someone) good*, and in *do your best* (try as hard as you can).

L.e: My neighbour did me a big favour and fed my cat while I was away. The storm did a lot of damage to the roof. A walk in the fresh air will do you good. We've done business with that firm for years. Don't worry about the result – just do your best.

L.x: I'll *do my best* (not *make my best*) to finish on time.

L.h: C Choosing between make and do

L.p: A useful rule: *make* when something new results (a cake, a plan, a mess, a fortune); *do* when you perform an activity or job (the ironing, an exercise, a course). The rule doesn't always work, so learn the common combinations as fixed phrases.

L.e: We made a mess in the kitchen, so we did the cleaning afterwards. She made a fortune from her app. He's doing a course in photography.

units.sub: go bald, become extinct, fall ill

L.p: *Go* is used for many changes in people and things, often unwanted ones: people *go grey*, *go bald*, *go deaf* or *blind* as they get older; a face *goes red* with embarrassment; milk *goes sour*; a business *goes bankrupt*; a plan *goes wrong*; a person *goes missing*.

L.e: My dad started going bald in his thirties. Grandma has gone a bit deaf, so speak clearly. Leave the milk out and it'll go sour. Everything went wrong on our first day. A climber has gone missing in the mountains. When the teacher called his name, his face went bright red.

L.p: *Turn* is common with colours and with weather: leaves *turn* brown, the sky *turns* orange, the weather *turns cold*. It is also used for ages: *turn thirty*. *Grow* suggests a slow change: *grow old*, *grow tired of*, *grow dark*.

L.e: In October the leaves turn gold and red. The weather turned cold overnight. My brother turns forty next week. As the evening went on, the sky grew dark. I soon grew tired of the city.

L.p: In speech, people often use *get* for changes of state: *get angry*, *get bored*, *get married*, *get lost*. In essays and formal writing, *become* sounds better, and with some words *get* is not possible at all: a species *becomes extinct*, a singer *becomes famous*, a policy *becomes unpopular*, families *become homeless*.

L.e: The dodo became extinct in the seventeenth century. After losing his job, he became homeless. The small bakery became famous for its pies. The kids got bored halfway through the film. We got lost on the way to the hotel.

L.x: The species *became extinct* (not *got extinct*) a hundred years ago.

L.p: *Fall* describes changes into a state: *fall ill*, *fall asleep*, *fall silent*, *fall in love*. *Come* is used in a few fixed phrases: a dream *comes true*, a knot or screw *comes loose*, a shoelace *comes undone*.

L.e: She fell ill the day before the wedding. I fell asleep on the sofa. The room fell silent when he walked in. Her dream of owning a horse finally came true. One of the wheels came loose.

units.sub: have fun, take action, pay a compliment

L.p: *Have* combines with many nouns for experiences and actions: *have fun*, *have a good time*, *have a look*, *have a go* (try), *have a word with* someone (talk briefly, often about a problem), *have an argument*, *have difficulty* (*in*) *doing* something, *have an impact on*.

L.e: We had great fun at the carnival. Can I have a look at your photos? Let me have a go at the puzzle. Could I have a word with you after class? I had difficulty finding a parking space. Social media has had a huge impact on politics.

L.p: *Take* often appears in collocations about decisions and responsibilities: *take action* (do something to deal with a problem), *take a risk*, *take responsibility for*, *take part in*, *take advantage of*, *take place* (happen), *take care of*, *take notes*.

L.e: The council must take action to reduce traffic. Starting a business means taking a risk. The manager took responsibility for the mistake. Thousands of people took part in the march. The concert will take place in the park. Take advantage of the sunny weather and go out!

L.p: *Pay* is used with attention and some kinds of respect: *pay attention*, *pay a compliment*, *pay a visit*, *pay tribute to*, *pay the price* (suffer the consequences). *Give* goes with *a speech*, *a lecture*, *an example*, *a hand* (help) and *someone a call*.

L.e: He paid me a lovely compliment on my cooking. We paid a visit to my grandmother on Sunday. The mayor paid tribute to the volunteers. If you don't revise, you'll pay the price in the exam. Could you give me a hand with these boxes? I'll give you a call tomorrow.

L.x: She *paid me a compliment* (not *made me a compliment*) on my dress.

units.sub: close a meeting, antique furniture, only child

L.p: *Close* and *shut* often mean the same with physical things: you can *close* or *shut* a door, a window or your eyes. But with abstract or formal things, only *close* is used: you *close a meeting*, *close a bank account*, *close a deal* (finish an agreement successfully) and *close a road*.

L.e: The chair closed the meeting at six o'clock. I closed my old bank account and opened a new one. After months of talks, the two firms closed the deal. Police closed the road after the accident. Please shut the gate behind you.

L.x: The chairperson *closed the meeting* (not *shut the meeting*) with a short speech.

L.p: These words all suggest age but have different partners. *Old* is general: an *old friend* (someone you have known for a long time). *Ancient* is for very distant times: *ancient history*, *ancient ruins*. *Antique* describes valuable old objects: *antique furniture*, an *antique clock*. *Elderly* is a polite word for old people: *elderly relatives*.

L.e: I met an old friend from school at the station. Tourists flock to see the ancient ruins. The shop sells antique furniture and old maps. Many elderly residents rely on the bus service.

L.p: An *only child* has no brothers or sisters. A *single parent* brings up children without a partner, and a *single room* is for one person. You *live alone* when nobody else lives with you, which is not the same as feeling *lonely* (unhappy because you are without company).

L.e: As an only child, I spent a lot of time with adults. My cousin is a single parent with two boys. I'd like a single room for three nights. My grandmother has lived alone since my grandfather died, but she's rarely lonely.

units.sub: gain power, achieve your goals, defeat an opponent

L.p: These verbs all mean getting something, but they have different partners. You *gain* things gradually: *gain power*, *gain experience*, *gain weight*, *gain confidence*. You *win* in competitions and contests: *win a prize*, *win a match*, *win an election*, *win an award*. You *earn* things through work or good behaviour: *earn money*, *earn a living*, *earn respect*.

L.e: The party gained power after a long period in opposition. A summer job is a good way to gain experience. Our school won an award for its garden. She earns a living as a translator. The new coach soon earned the players' respect.

L.x: He *earns a good salary* (not *wins a good salary*) as an engineer.

L.p: You *achieve your goals* or *achieve success*; you *reach a target*, *reach an agreement* or *reach a conclusion*; you *accomplish a task* or *accomplish a mission* (complete something difficult).

L.e: With hard work, you can achieve your goals. Sales reached their target in November. After hours of discussion, the two sides reached an agreement. The team accomplished the task in record time.

L.p: You *defeat* or *beat* an opponent, a rival or an enemy (*defeat* is more formal), but you *win* a game, race or battle. So: City *beat* United; City *won* the match. Armies *defeat* their enemies; ideas can also be defeated: *defeat a proposal* (vote against it successfully).

L.e: The young player defeated the champion in straight sets. We beat our rivals 3–1 and won the cup. Parliament defeated the proposal by twenty votes.

L.x: Our team *beat* (not *won*) the visitors by two goals.

units.sub: sunny smile, ideas flow, heated discussion

L.p: English often describes happiness and hope in terms of light and good weather: a *sunny smile*, a *sunny disposition* (a cheerful character), a *bright future*, a face that *lights up* or is *beaming*. Sadness is dark or cloudy: *a gloomy face*, *dark days*, *a cloud* over something.

L.e: The receptionist greeted us with a sunny smile. With her talent, she has a bright future ahead of her. His face lit up when he saw the cake. The factory closure cast a cloud over the town.

L.p: We talk about ideas and words as if they were water: *ideas flow* when you are creative; you get *a flood of* letters or complaints; the conversation *dries up* when nobody has anything to say; information *leaks* out; a meeting has a *stream of* visitors.

L.e: Once we started brainstorming, the ideas began to flow. The programme received a flood of complaints. After ten minutes the conversation dried up. Details of the plan leaked out before the announcement.

L.p: Strong feelings, especially anger and excitement, are described as heat: a *heated discussion* (an angry one), *boiling with rage*, a *burning ambition*, things *cool down* or *heat up*. Lack of feeling is cold: a *cold stare*, a *frosty reception*.

L.e: The council meeting turned into a heated discussion. He was boiling with rage after the referee's decision. She has a burning ambition to become a pilot. Let's wait until everyone has cooled down. The new manager got a frosty reception from the staff.

units.sub: strong wind, blanket of fog, river bursts its banks

L.p: Rain is *heavy* or *light*, and very heavy rain is *torrential*. Wind is *strong* (not *heavy*), and the strongest are *gale-force winds*; when wind becomes weaker it *drops*, and when it gets stronger it *picks up*. Sunshine is *bright*, and very good weather can be *glorious*; extremely hot weather is *scorching*.

L.e: Torrential rain flooded the main road. A strong wind blew the umbrella out of my hand. The wind dropped in the evening, so we went sailing. We spent a glorious afternoon on the beach in bright sunshine. It was scorching in the city, so we stayed indoors.

L.x: Hold on to your hat – there's a *strong wind* (not *heavy wind*) today.

L.p: Fog can be *thick* or *dense*; a large area of fog or snow covering the ground can be called *a blanket of* fog or snow. Fog *lifts* or *clears* when it goes away. Snow *falls* and *settles* (stays on the ground); invisible ice on roads is *black ice*. A cold, dry, clear morning is *crisp*.

L.e: The town woke up under a blanket of fog. By lunchtime the fog had lifted. Snow fell all night, but it didn't settle. Drivers should watch out for black ice. It was a crisp winter morning, perfect for a walk.

L.p: After heavy rain, a river may *burst its banks*, and sudden local floods are *flash floods*. A storm *hits* a place; lightning *strikes* something. A long period of very hot weather is a *heatwave*, and a long period without rain is a *drought*.

L.e: The river burst its banks and flooded the village. A severe storm hit the south coast last night. Lightning struck a tree in the park. During the heatwave, temperatures reached 38 degrees. Farmers are worried about the drought.

units.sub: tiring journey, aisle seat, family-run hotel

L.p: A journey can be *long*, *tiring*, *exhausting* or *uneventful* (nothing special happened). You *set off on* a journey. Flights can be *smooth* or *bumpy*; if you have to change planes or trains, you need to *catch your connection* and hope you don't *miss* it.

L.e: After a tiring journey, we went straight to bed. The flight was smooth until we started to land. Our train was late, so we missed our connection in Paris. It was an uneventful drive, apart from one wrong turning.

L.h: B On the plane or train

L.p: On a plane, you can ask for an *aisle seat* (next to the passageway) or a *window seat*. You *board* a plane or train; a service can be *delayed* or *cancelled*. It's usually cheaper to *book in advance*, and a *return ticket* covers the journey there and back.

L.e: I always ask for an aisle seat on long flights. Passengers were asked to board the plane through gate 12. Our flight was delayed by three hours. If you book in advance, you can save a lot of money.

L.x: We *boarded the plane* (not *climbed on the plane*) just before midnight.

L.p: A small *family-run hotel* is owned and managed by one family. *Budget accommodation* is cheap; a hotel with no free rooms is *fully booked*. Rooms may have a *sea view*, and an *en-suite* room has its own bathroom. You *check in* when you arrive and *check out* when you leave.

L.e: We stayed in a lovely family-run hotel near the harbour. All the hotels in the centre were fully booked. Could we have a room with a sea view, please? Guests must check out by eleven.

units.sub: surrounding countryside, well worth seeing, off the beaten track

L.p: Collocations for countryside often combine an adjective with a landscape noun: *rolling hills* (gently rising and falling), *breathtaking scenery*, *dense forest*, a *winding path*, a *rugged coastline* (rocky and wild), *unspoilt beaches* (not changed by tourism). From a high place you can see *the surrounding countryside*.

L.e: From the castle walls there's a wonderful view of the surrounding countryside. The road follows a rugged coastline with breathtaking scenery. We walked along a winding path through dense forest. The island still has unspoilt beaches.

L.p: Places that are *well worth seeing* or *well worth a visit* are very interesting. Somewhere *off the beaten track* is far from the usual tourist routes. Visitors *go hiking* or *go for a ramble* (a long walk), *take in the view* (look at it with pleasure) and explore *picturesque villages*.

L.e: The old mill is well worth a visit. We found a tiny café off the beaten track. On Sunday we went for a ramble along the river. We stopped at the top to take in the view. The region is full of picturesque villages.

L.p: Farmers *grow crops* such as wheat and barley and *keep* or *raise* animals. Sheep and cows *graze* in fields; crops are *harvested* at the end of summer. Land that is good for farming is *fertile*; poor land is *barren*.

L.e: The valley has fertile soil, so farmers grow crops all year. Cows were grazing peacefully by the river. The grapes are harvested in September.

units.sub: lined with shops, sprawling city, volume of traffic

L.p: A *sprawling city* has spread over a large area without much planning. Streets can be *bustling* (busy and lively) or *deserted*; they may be *lined with* shops, cafés or trees. Many towns have a *historic centre* or a *quaint old town* (attractive in an old-fashioned way), as well as *residential areas* and *industrial estates*.

L.e: Mexico City is a vast, sprawling city. The main square is lined with cafés. We wandered through the bustling streets of the market. The historic centre is closed to cars. Most people live in residential areas on the edge of town.

L.p: The *volume of traffic* (the amount of it) causes *traffic congestion* and *air pollution*, especially during *rush-hour traffic*. Some districts are *run-down* (in poor condition), and big cities may suffer from *inner-city problems* such as poor housing and crime.

L.e: The volume of traffic has doubled in ten years. Traffic congestion is worst on Friday afternoons. Air pollution in the city centre is above safe levels. The council plans to regenerate the run-down areas near the station.

L.p: Many cities are improving *public transport*, creating *pedestrian zones* (areas where cars are not allowed) and *cycle lanes*. If something is *within walking distance*, you can easily walk there.

L.e: Public transport here is cheap and reliable. The new pedestrian zone has made shopping more pleasant. Our hotel is within walking distance of the old town. More cycle lanes would encourage people to leave their cars at home.

L.x: Everything is *within walking distance* (not *in walking distance*) of the hotel.

units.sub: have a vivid imagination, lose your patience, set a good example

L.p: Character collocations often use *have*: *have a vivid imagination* (be very creative), *have a good sense of humour*, *have a quick temper* (get angry easily). Adverbs strengthen character adjectives: *painfully shy*, *fiercely independent*, *refreshingly honest*. Someone with a *strong personality* has firm opinions and a big influence on others.

L.e: My niece has a vivid imagination – she invents stories about everything. Our new boss has a great sense of humour. He was painfully shy as a teenager. My grandmother is fiercely independent and refuses any help. It was refreshingly honest of her to admit the mistake.

L.p: When something makes you angry after a long time, you *lose your patience* or *lose your temper*; if you stay calm, you *keep your temper* or *keep calm*. Adults should *set a good example* to children. You *show respect* for people you admire, and you *take offence* when you feel insulted.

L.e: After an hour in the queue, I finally lost my patience. Try not to lose your temper with the children. Teachers need to set a good example. Visitors should show respect for local customs. I didn't mean to be rude – please don't take offence.

L.x: She *lost her temper* (not *lost her nerves*) and started shouting.

L.p: You can *get into* a habit or *fall into* a habit (start doing it without planning to), *break a habit* or *kick a habit* (stop, informal), and describe some habits as *bad habits* or *nervous habits*, such as biting your nails.

L.e: I've got into the habit of checking my phone at night. Smoking is a hard habit to break. Biting your nails is a nervous habit.

units.sub: slender waist, immaculately groomed, broad shoulders

L.p: Many appearance collocations are adjective + noun: a *slender waist*, *broad shoulders*, *chubby cheeks*, *piercing blue eyes* (bright and seeming to look right through you), a *pale complexion*, *shoulder-length hair*, *thinning hair* (becoming less thick).

L.e: The dancer had a slender waist and long arms. The rugby player has very broad shoulders. The baby has chubby cheeks and curly hair. She looked at me with piercing blue eyes. My uncle's hair is thinning on top.

L.p: Adverbs combine with appearance adjectives: *strikingly beautiful*, *ruggedly handsome* (attractive in a strong, outdoor way), *smartly dressed*, *scruffily dressed*, *immaculately groomed* (with perfect hair and clothes). Your weight can change: you *put on weight* or *lose weight*.

L.e: The host was immaculately groomed in a grey suit. Everyone at the interview was smartly dressed. The actor is ruggedly handsome. He has put on weight since he stopped playing football. She lost a lot of weight after changing her diet.

L.x: I've *put on weight* (not *taken weight*) over the holidays.

L.p: You *keep fit* or *stay in shape* by exercising; if you are *in good shape*, your body is healthy and strong. Someone who looks *the picture of health* looks very well.

L.e: My grandparents keep fit by swimming twice a week. You're in good shape for your age! After her holiday she looked the picture of health.

units.sub: distant cousin, expecting a baby, stable home

L.p: Your *immediate family* are your parents, children, brothers and sisters; your *extended family* includes aunts, uncles, cousins and grandparents. A *close relative* is a near family member; a *distant cousin* or *distant relative* is only loosely related. Family members can be *on their father's side* or *on their mother's side*.

L.e: Only immediate family were invited to the funeral. Our extended family meets every summer. I discovered that the famous singer is a distant cousin of mine. My grandparents on my mother's side live in Wales.

L.h: B Starting and raising a family

L.p: A woman who is pregnant is *expecting a baby*; she later *gives birth to* a son or daughter. Couples *start a family* when they have their first child, and parents *bring up* or *raise* children. A *single parent* raises children alone.

L.e: Our neighbours are expecting a baby in the spring. Last night she gave birth to twins. They hope to find a bigger flat before they start a family. My grandmother brought up six children on her own.

L.x: She *gave birth to* (not *made birth to*) a healthy boy.

L.p: Children grow up best in a *stable home*; a *broken home* is one where the parents have separated. Families meet at *family gatherings*; relatives who look alike share a *family resemblance*; a talent or illness that many members have *runs in the family*. Strong connections between relatives are *family ties*.

L.e: Every child deserves a stable home. Christmas is our big family gathering. There's a strong family resemblance between the three sisters. Musical talent runs in the family. Family ties are very important in many cultures.

units.sub: casual acquaintance, love at first sight, drift apart

L.p: A *casual acquaintance* is someone you know slightly; a *lifelong friend* is someone you have known since childhood; a *mutual friend* is a friend of two people. You *make friends* with people, *strike up a friendship* (begin one, often by chance) and try to *keep in touch*. If you stop contacting someone, you *lose touch* with them.

L.e: He's not really a friend, just a casual acquaintance. Kate and I are lifelong friends. We met through a mutual friend. I struck up a friendship with the woman next to me on the train. We lost touch after university, but we're back in touch now.

L.p: When two people fall in love immediately, it's *love at first sight*. You *fall madly in love*, *ask someone out*, *go on a date*, and perhaps *get engaged* and married. A *steady relationship* is stable and long-term. When a relationship ends, people *break up* or *split up*.

L.e: My grandparents say it was love at first sight. He finally asked her out after weeks of chatting. They went on their first date to an Italian restaurant. After three years, they got engaged on a mountaintop. They split up last year but are still friends.

L.p: Couples and friends sometimes *have a row* (an argument, informal). People who slowly become less close *drift apart*. You *patch up* a quarrel when you become friends again. A relationship full of arguments is *stormy*; if two people are *not on speaking terms*, they refuse to talk to each other.

L.e: They had a terrible row about money. We drifted apart after she moved abroad. The two brothers finally patched up their quarrel. Their marriage was stormy from the start. My neighbours haven't been on speaking terms for years.

L.x: We *had a row* (not *made a row*) about the washing-up.

units.sub: move into a flat, spacious living room, do up a house

L.p: You *rent a flat* or *buy a house*, then *move into* it; when you leave, you *move out of* it. People *put a house on the market* when they want to sell it. A flat may be *furnished* or *unfurnished*, and rented homes often require a *deposit*. Homes in a quiet area are in a *residential street*.

L.e: We moved into our new flat last weekend. They put their house on the market in spring. The landlord asked for a deposit of two months' rent. We'd prefer an unfurnished flat in a quiet residential street.

L.x: We *moved into* (not *moved to*) the flat on Saturday and started unpacking.

L.p: Rooms can be *spacious* (large and comfortable), *cramped* (too small), *cosy* (warm and comfortable), *airy* (light and fresh) or *poky* (small and unpleasant, informal). A house may have an *open-plan kitchen*, *fitted wardrobes* and *high ceilings*; a room with lots of sunshine *gets the sun* or *faces south*.

L.e: The flat has a spacious living room and an open-plan kitchen. My student room was cramped but cosy. The bedroom is light and airy, with fitted wardrobes. Our garden faces south, so it gets the sun all afternoon.

L.p: People *do up* an old house (repair and decorate it, informal), *redecorate* a room, *build an extension*, *knock down a wall* or *put up shelves*. A house that needs a lot of work is *in need of renovation*.

L.e: We bought an old cottage in need of renovation and spent two years doing it up. They knocked down a wall to make the kitchen bigger. My dad put up shelves in every room.

units.sub: nourishing meal, spoil your appetite, dying of hunger

L.p: A *nourishing meal* is full of what your body needs; a *light meal* or *snack* is small; a *three-course meal* has a starter, main course and dessert. Food can be *home-made*, *mouth-watering* (looking or smelling delicious) or *stodgy* (heavy). You *cook a meal*, *prepare a meal* or, more informally, *rustle up* something quick.

L.e: After the hike we cooked a hot, nourishing meal. The restaurant serves a three-course meal for £25. The smell of home-made bread was mouth-watering. I rustled up some pasta with what was in the fridge.

L.p: Informally, people *are dying of hunger* or *are starving* when very hungry. Eating between meals can *spoil your appetite*; a walk can *give you an appetite*; if you're ill, you may *lose your appetite*. People with big appetites have *a healthy appetite*.

L.e: When's dinner? I'm dying of hunger! Don't eat crisps now – you'll spoil your appetite. The sea air gave us a huge appetite. Since she's been ill, she's lost her appetite. Teenage boys usually have a healthy appetite.

L.x: You'll *spoil your appetite* (not *break your appetite*) if you eat sweets before dinner.

L.p: Tea and coffee can be *strong* or *weak*; *sparkling* or *still* water; a *soft drink* has no alcohol. You *quench your thirst* with a cold drink. Someone who doesn't drink alcohol is *teetotal*.

L.e: I like my tea weak with lots of milk. Would you like still or sparkling water? Nothing quenches your thirst like cold water after a run. Soft drinks contain a lot of sugar.

units.sub: film critic, go on the stage, gripping plot

L.p: A *film critic* writes reviews. A film can *get good reviews* or *bad reviews*, *star* famous actors and be *set in* a particular place or time. Popular films *break box-office records*. Actors *play a part* or *a role*; a *leading role* is the main one, and a *supporting role* is smaller.

L.e: The film got excellent reviews from the critics. It's set in Edinburgh in the 1950s. Her latest film broke box-office records. He played the leading role in a historical drama.

L.p: Someone who becomes an actor *goes on the stage*. Theatres *put on a play* or *stage a production*; a play *opens* on its first night and may *run* for months. At the end, the audience *gives the actors a standing ovation*.

L.e: She went on the stage at the age of sixteen. The local drama group is putting on a comedy. The musical opened last week and will run until June. The cast got a standing ovation.

L.x: The school is *putting on a play* (not *making a play*) for the parents.

L.p: A book can have a *gripping plot* (very exciting), *well-drawn characters* or a *happy ending*. People *publish* books, which may *become bestsellers*; readers *can't put a book down* when it's really exciting. A book that has been *made into a film* is an *adaptation*.

L.e: The novel has a gripping plot and a surprising ending. It became a bestseller within weeks. I couldn't put it down! The book has been made into a TV series.

units.sub: give a performance, go on tour, strum a guitar

L.p: Musicians *play* instruments, but some instruments have more specific verbs: you *strum a guitar* (brush your fingers over the strings to play chords), *beat a drum* and *blow a trumpet*. You *play by ear* if you play without written music, and you *play in tune* or *out of tune*. A singer *sings in tune* or *hits the high notes*.

L.e: He sat by the fire strumming his guitar. The choir sang beautifully in tune. My grandmother can play any song by ear. The violinist was slightly out of tune in the second piece.

L.p: Musicians *give a performance* or *give a concert*; a band *goes on tour* and *plays to a packed audience*. A new song can *top the charts* (be number one) and a successful album *goes platinum* (sells a very large number). Fans *queue for tickets*, and popular concerts *sell out*.

L.e: The pianist gave a stunning performance. The band is going on tour in Asia next year. They played to a packed audience in Dublin. Their first single topped the charts. Tickets for the festival sold out in minutes.

L.x: The orchestra *gave a concert* (not *made a concert*) in the cathedral.

L.p: Listeners can *turn the music up* or *turn it down*, *have the radio on*, and describe music as *catchy* (easy to remember), *soothing* or *deafening*. A song you can't stop thinking about is *stuck in your head*.

L.e: Could you turn the music down? I always have the radio on when I cook. That song is so catchy – it's been stuck in my head all day. Soothing music helps me sleep.

units.sub: go snowboarding, take a penalty, set a record

L.p: We *go* + *-ing* for many activities, especially outdoor ones: *go snowboarding*, *go cycling*, *go sailing*. We *play* games with a ball or against an opponent: *play tennis*, *play chess*. We *do* other activities, especially without a ball: *do judo*, *do gymnastics*, *do yoga*.

L.e: Every winter we go snowboarding in the Alps. My son plays football twice a week. She does judo after school. I've started doing yoga to help my back.

L.x: I *do yoga* (not *play yoga*) every morning.

L.p: Players *score a goal* or *take a penalty*; a team can *win*, *lose* or *draw* a match. Athletes *break a record* or *set a new record*; they *qualify for* a final and *compete in* a tournament. The person who controls a game is the *referee*, who may *award a free kick* or *send a player off*.

L.e: He took the penalty and scored in the last minute. The match ended in a draw. She set a new national record in the 400 metres. Our team qualified for the final. The referee sent two players off.

L.p: Athletes *go into training*, *train hard* and try to *stay in shape*. You can *pull a muscle* if you don't *warm up* properly. A good result is a *personal best* (the best you have ever done).

L.e: She's gone into training for the marathon. Always warm up before you run, or you might pull a muscle. I ran a personal best in yesterday's race.

units.sub: catch a cold, vigorous exercise, be taken ill

L.p: You *catch a cold* or *catch flu*; you *come down with* something (start to get ill); you *pick up a virus* (informal); and someone may *be taken ill* suddenly, often in a public place. Children may *run a temperature* (have a fever).

L.e: I caught a cold on the plane. She came down with flu the day before her exams. A passenger was taken ill during the flight. My son is running a temperature, so he's staying at home.

L.x: I think I've *caught a cold* (not *taken a cold*).

L.p: Doctors *prescribe medicine* or *antibiotics*; you *take* medicine and *make a full recovery*. Patients *have an operation*; surgeons *perform* it. If your health gets worse, your condition *deteriorates*; if it gets better, it *improves*. A serious illness may leave you *seriously ill*, but you hope to be *back on your feet* soon.

L.e: The doctor prescribed antibiotics for my chest infection. She had an operation on her knee last month. Doctors expect him to make a full recovery. His condition improved overnight. You'll be back on your feet in no time.

L.p: To stay healthy, you can *take regular exercise* (or *vigorous exercise*, which makes you breathe hard), *eat a balanced diet*, *get enough sleep* and *cut down on* sugar or salt. Smokers are advised to *give up smoking*.

L.e: Doctors recommend thirty minutes of vigorous exercise three times a week. Try to eat a balanced diet. I've cut down on coffee. My dad gave up smoking ten years ago.

units.sub: refine your search, open an attachment, go viral

L.p: You *go online*, *browse the internet* and *do a search* (or *run a search*). When a search brings back thousands of pages, you can *refine your search* – narrow it with extra keywords or filters. You *click on a link*, *bookmark a page* you want to return to, and *download* or *upload* files.

L.e: I did a quick search for cheap flights. There were thousands of results, so I refined my search. Click on the link at the bottom of the page. I bookmarked the recipe so I could find it later.

L.p: You *send* or *forward* an email, *attach a file*, and the receiver *opens the attachment*. You *reply to* a message, *delete* spam and *check your inbox*. If an email address is wrong, the message *bounces back*.

L.e: I'll forward you the email from the manager. Don't open an attachment from someone you don't know. I check my inbox first thing every morning. My message bounced back because I'd typed the address wrong.

L.x: Please *reply to my email* (not *answer to my email*) by Friday.

L.p: People *post* photos and *share* links; a video that spreads quickly *goes viral*. You *set up an account*, *log in* with a *strong password* and *change your privacy settings*. Criminals may try to *hack into* an account.

L.e: Her dance video went viral overnight. I set up an account on the new site. Always use a strong password. Someone hacked into my email and sent messages to all my contacts.

units.sub: do research, attend a lecture, first draft

L.p: Students *attend lectures* and *seminars*, *take notes*, *do research* and *write an essay* or *assignment*. They must *meet a deadline* and may *ask for an extension* if they need more time. At the end, they *sit* or *take an exam* and hope to *pass* with good marks.

L.e: About two hundred students attended the lecture. I take notes on my laptop. We're doing research on local history. I asked my tutor for an extension because I was ill. She passed all her exams with high marks.

L.x: I have to *do research* (not *make research*) for my dissertation.

L.p: Writers usually *make a plan* and *write a first draft*, then *revise* it into a *final draft*. Good essays *develop an argument*, *give examples* and *cite sources*. Copying without acknowledgement is *plagiarism* and can lead to students *failing* a course.

L.e: Write a first draft quickly, then improve it. My tutor said my essay needed to develop the argument more clearly. Make sure you cite your sources correctly.

L.p: Learners *acquire knowledge*, *master a skill*, *broaden their horizons* (learn about new things) and *make progress*. A subject that you find hard may be a *steep learning curve*. Students who stop a course early *drop out*.

L.e: Living abroad really broadened my horizons. It took her years to master the violin. The first month in the new job was a steep learning curve. A few students drop out every year.

units.sub: target audience, prepare handouts, public speaking

L.p: First think about your *target audience* (the people you want to reach). Then *do your research*, *plan your talk*, *prepare your slides* and *prepare handouts* (printed summaries). It helps to *rehearse your presentation* several times.

L.e: Who is your target audience – students or parents? I spent the weekend preparing my slides. Don't forget to prepare handouts for everyone. Rehearse your presentation in front of a friend.

L.p: Speakers *give* (or *deliver*) *a presentation*, *make a point*, *draw attention to* key information and *keep to time*. Good speakers *make eye contact* with the audience and *invite questions* at the end. Many people are nervous about *public speaking*.

L.e: I have to give a presentation to the board on Monday. She made an important point about costs. Try to make eye contact with people in the room. At the end, he invited questions from the audience. Public speaking terrifies me.

L.x: Tomorrow I'm *giving a presentation* (not *making a speech presentation*) on renewable energy.

L.p: Listeners may *ask a question*, *raise a point* or *give feedback*. A successful talk *holds the audience's attention* (keeps them interested).

L.e: Several people raised interesting points afterwards. My manager gave me useful feedback. Her talk held the audience's attention from start to finish.

units.sub: high-powered job, hand in your notice, earn a living

L.p: A *high-powered job* is important and demanding; a *dead-end job* has no future; a *steady job* is secure. You *apply for a job*, *get a job* or *land a job* (informal: get one you wanted), *take on* responsibilities and *pursue a career* in a particular field.

L.e: She left a high-powered job in banking to become a teacher. I don't want to stay in a dead-end job. He finally landed a job with a film company. My sister is pursuing a career in medicine.

L.p: People *work long hours*, *work overtime* or *work shifts*. Some have *flexible working hours* or *work from home*. Workers *get a pay rise*, *take time off* and *take early retirement*.

L.e: Nurses often work long hours. I worked overtime every evening last week. My company lets us work from home on Fridays. I got a pay rise after my review. She took early retirement at fifty-five.

L.x: I'd like to *take time off* (not *make time off*) in August.

L.p: When you decide to leave, you *hand in your notice* or *resign*. Companies *lay off staff* when business is bad, and an employee who does something seriously wrong *gets the sack* (informal) or *is dismissed*.

L.e: I handed in my notice yesterday – I start my new job next month. The factory laid off 200 staff. He got the sack for being late every day.

L.h: A Starting and running a business

L.p: Entrepreneurs *set up a business* (or *start up* a company), *draw up a business plan* and *raise capital* (find money to invest). Once they are trading, they *run* or *manage the business*, *employ staff* and hope to *make a profit*. A company that is doing well *expands* or *goes from strength to strength*.

L.e: Two friends set up a business selling bicycles. You'll need to draw up a business plan before you talk to the bank. They raised capital from family and friends. The café has gone from strength to strength.

L.p: Companies *launch a product* (introduce it to the market), *market* it, and try to *increase sales* and *gain market share*. They compete with *rival companies* and *competitors*. A company that is first in a market is a *market leader*.

L.e: The company will launch the new phone in September. Sales increased by 15% last year. A rival company has cut its prices. They are the market leader in sports shoes.

L.x: The firm will *launch its new product* (not *throw its new product*) next month.

L.p: A business can *suffer losses*, *go out of business* or *go bankrupt*. It may need to *cut costs* or be *taken over* by a larger company. Two companies that join *merge*.

L.e: The airline suffered heavy losses during the crisis. Several local shops have gone out of business. The company is cutting costs by closing offices. The small brewery was taken over by an international group.

units.sub: key factor, challenge a theory, carry out research

L.p: Researchers *carry out research*, *conduct a survey* or *an experiment*, *collect data* and *analyse the results*. They *put forward a theory* or *a hypothesis* and *test* it. Other scholars may *challenge a theory* (question whether it is right) or *support* it with new *evidence*.

L.e: The team carried out research in twelve schools. We conducted a survey of 500 drivers. The data were collected over three years. Her findings challenge the theory that bees avoid cities. New evidence supports the original hypothesis.

L.x: The scientists *carried out an experiment* (not *made an experiment*) on sleep.

L.p: Academic writers highlight what matters with collocations such as *a key factor*, *a crucial role*, *a major issue*, *a central theme*, *a significant difference*. They *play a part in* or *have an effect on* something, and they *draw attention to* points that readers should notice.

L.e: Cost was a key factor in the decision. Parents play a crucial role in a child's education. There was no significant difference between the two groups. Climate change is the central theme of the book. The report draws attention to the lack of housing.

L.p: Researchers *obtain results*, *reach a conclusion* and *present their findings*. Results may *confirm* or *contradict* earlier work. A study can *shed light on* (help explain) a problem.

L.e: The results confirm what earlier studies found. The study sheds new light on how children learn to read. She will present her findings at a conference in June.

units.sub: make reference to, argue convincingly, research suggests

L.p: Academic writers *make reference to* other works, *quote* or *cite* authors and *draw on* (use) earlier studies. They describe what sources say with reporting verbs: *research suggests that…*, *the evidence indicates…*, *the author claims / argues / maintains that…*.

L.e: The essay makes reference to several recent studies. Research suggests that bilingual children are better at switching tasks. The author argues that cities should ban cars from the centre. My chapter draws on interviews with forty teachers.

L.p: Writers *argue convincingly* (in a way that persuades) or *put forward an argument*; they *present a case* for or against something and *support their claims* with evidence. An argument can be *strong*, *weak*, *persuasive* or *flawed*. A careful writer *takes into account* other points of view.

L.e: She argues convincingly that the tax is unfair. The report presents a strong case for building more homes. Support your claims with examples. His argument is flawed because it ignores the cost. The study takes into account differences in age.

L.x: The writer *argues convincingly* (not *argues persuasively strong*) that schools should start later.

L.p: Academic English often avoids sounding too certain: *it would appear that…*, *it is widely believed that…*, *there is little evidence that…*. To finish, writers *draw conclusions*, *make recommendations* and *point out the limitations* of their work.

L.e: It would appear that the treatment is effective. There is little evidence that the policy reduced crime. Finally, the authors point out the limitations of their small sample and make recommendations for further research.

units.sub: break the law, bend the rules, fair trial

L.p: Parliaments *pass a law* or *introduce new legislation*; police *enforce the law*. People who obey the law are *law-abiding*; those who don't *break the law*. You *obey* or *follow the rules*; if you *bend the rules*, you change them slightly to suit a situation. A law can be *strict* or *relaxed*, and it may *come into force* on a particular date.

L.e: The government passed a law banning smoking in cars with children. Parking on the pavement is breaking the law. The receptionist bent the rules and let us check in early. The new speed limits come into force in January.

L.x: Driving without insurance is *breaking the law* (not *cutting the law*).

L.p: A suspect is *charged with* a crime and *stands trial*. Everyone has the right to a *fair trial*. Lawyers *present the evidence*, witnesses *give evidence*, and the jury *reaches a verdict*. The judge then *passes sentence*.

L.e: He was charged with theft and will stand trial in May. Every defendant deserves a fair trial. Three witnesses gave evidence on the first day. The judge passed a sentence of four years.

L.p: Criminals *receive a sentence*: *a prison sentence*, *a fine*, *community service*. A judge may *impose a fine* or a *suspended sentence* (one that is only served if the person commits another crime). Prisoners *serve a sentence* and may be *released on parole* early.

L.e: The driver received a heavy fine and lost his licence. She was sentenced to 200 hours of community service. He served six years of a ten-year sentence and was released on parole.

units.sub: hardened criminal, juvenile crime, tackle crime

L.p: People *commit a crime* or *commit an offence*; a *petty crime* is a minor one, such as shoplifting, while a *serious crime* might be murder or armed robbery. A *hardened criminal* has committed many crimes and is unlikely to change. Crimes by young people are *juvenile crime*; a first-time offender has no previous record.

L.e: Most petty crime in the town happens at night. The police described him as a hardened criminal. Juvenile crime has fallen since the youth centre opened. Armed robbery is a serious crime.

L.p: Police *investigate a crime*, *look for clues*, *interview witnesses* and *make an arrest*. They may *issue a warrant* to search a house or *launch an appeal* for information. A crime that has not been solved remains *unsolved*.

L.e: Detectives are investigating a series of burglaries. Officers made three arrests after the match. Police have launched an appeal for witnesses. The case remains unsolved twenty years later.

L.x: The police *made an arrest* (not *did an arrest*) early this morning.

L.p: Governments and communities *tackle crime*, *crack down on* particular offences (deal with them strongly), *reduce the crime rate* and try to *prevent crime* through better lighting, education and jobs. Some people *turn to crime* because of poverty.

L.e: The new mayor promised to tackle crime in the city centre. Police are cracking down on drivers who use phones. Better street lighting helped reduce the crime rate. Many young people turn to crime when they can't find work.

units.sub: hit the headlines, hold talks, take hostage

L.p: A story *makes the news* or *hits the headlines* when it becomes widely reported; a *news story* can *break* (become public for the first time). Newspapers *carry a story* or *run a story*; TV channels *give* an event *wide coverage*. The latest information is *breaking news*.

L.e: The singer's surprise wedding hit the headlines. The story broke late last night. Every paper carried the story on its front page. The election was given wide coverage on all channels.

L.p: Leaders *hold talks*, *reach an agreement* and *sign a deal*. Governments *announce plans*, *make a statement* or *issue a warning*. Politicians *come under pressure* to resign, and may *face criticism* from the public.

L.e: The two presidents held talks in Geneva. The minister made a statement to the press. Health officials have issued a warning about the heat. The minister came under pressure to resign after the scandal.

L.x: The leaders will *hold talks* (not *make talks*) next week.

L.p: Some news is about danger: gunmen *take people hostage*, and hostages are later *released*; people *are reported missing* or *are feared dead*; rescue teams *launch a search*. A disaster may *claim lives*.

L.e: Rebels took three aid workers hostage, but they were released after a week. Two climbers have been reported missing. The coastguard launched a search at dawn. The floods claimed more than twenty lives.

units.sub: squander money, price soars, go cheap

L.p: You *spend money on* things, *save money* or *put money aside* for the future. If you *squander money* or *waste money*, you spend it foolishly. People *live within their means* (spend no more than they earn) or *get into debt*. A large amount of money is *a small fortune*.

L.e: My brother squandered his savings on a sports car. We're trying to put money aside for a holiday. They got into debt after buying a big house. That painting must have cost a small fortune.

L.x: He *wastes money* (not *loses money*) on things he never uses.

L.p: Prices *rise*, *go up* or, when they rise very fast, *soar* or *rocket*; they *fall*, *go down*, *drop* or *plummet*. Something sold for less than usual *goes cheap* (informal) or is *a bargain*. A shop may *charge* a high price or *slash prices* (cut them a lot).

L.e: House prices soared last year. The price of petrol plummeted in spring. At the end of the market day, fruit goes cheap. The shop slashed its prices in the January sale. This jacket was a real bargain.

L.p: You *open* or *close a bank account*, *pay money into* it and *withdraw money* from it. You can *take out a loan* or *a mortgage* (to buy a house) and *pay it back* in *monthly instalments*. If you spend more than you have, you are *overdrawn*.

L.e: I opened a savings account for my daughter. She withdrew £200 from a cash machine. We took out a mortgage to buy our flat. I'm paying the loan back in monthly instalments.

units.sub: war breaks out, restore order, call a truce

L.p: War *breaks out* (starts suddenly); countries *declare war on* each other or *go to war*. Armies *launch an attack*, *invade a country* and *fight a battle*. Conflicts can *escalate* (become more serious). Civilians may *flee their homes* and become refugees.

L.e: War broke out between the two countries in 1914. The army launched an attack at dawn. Fighting escalated after the bombing of the capital. Thousands of families fled their homes.

L.x: War *broke out* (not *broke up*) in the north of the country.

L.p: Sides that want to stop fighting *call a truce* or *agree a ceasefire* (an agreement to stop shooting), *hold peace talks* and finally *sign a peace treaty*. A peacekeeping force may *restore order* (make a situation calm again) and *keep the peace*.

L.e: The rebels called a truce over the holiday. Both sides agreed a ceasefire. The peace talks lasted six months. The treaty was signed in a castle near the border. United Nations troops restored order in the city.

L.p: Countries *rebuild* cities and *rebuild their economy*; families *mourn the dead*; leaders *pay tribute to* those who *lost their lives*. Monuments are built to *commemorate* the fallen.

L.e: It took decades to rebuild the city after the war. A monument commemorates the soldiers who lost their lives. The president paid tribute to the victims.

units.sub: eradicate poverty, forced migration, climate change

L.p: International organisations aim to *eradicate poverty* (end it completely), *reduce inequality* and *provide aid*. Many people still *live in poverty* or *live below the poverty line*. Aid workers *distribute food* and *provide shelter* after disasters.

L.e: The charity's goal is to eradicate poverty in the region. Millions of people live below the poverty line. Volunteers distributed food and blankets. The organisation provides shelter for homeless families.

L.p: *Voluntary migration* is when people choose to move, for example for work; *forced migration* is when they have no choice, because of war, persecution or disaster. Refugees *seek asylum* in another country; governments *take in refugees* or *close their borders*.

L.e: Most migration to the cities has been voluntary, but the war caused forced migration on a huge scale. Thousands of families have sought asylum in neighbouring countries. Several countries agreed to take in refugees.

L.p: Global problems include *climate change*, *rising sea levels* and the *destruction of rainforests*. Countries promise to *cut carbon emissions*, *protect endangered species* and *tackle pollution*. Many animals are *facing extinction*.

L.e: Climate change is affecting farming everywhere. Rising sea levels threaten low-lying islands. The agreement commits countries to cut carbon emissions. Several species of frog are facing extinction.

units.sub: save time, ungodly hours, from dawn till dusk

L.p: Time is often treated like money: you *spend time*, *save time*, *waste time* and *make up for lost time*. You can *kill time* (do something unimportant while waiting), *find time* for something, or *run out of time*. When nobody is rushing you, you can *take your time*.

L.e: Booking online saves a lot of time. Don't waste time worrying about it. We played cards to kill time at the airport. I never seem to find time to read. Take your time – there's no rush.

L.x: We *spent* (not *passed*) a lot of time planning the trip.

L.p: Very early or very late times are *the early hours* (after midnight) or, informally, *ungodly hours* (unreasonably early or late). Something that goes on all day lasts *from dawn till dusk*. You can be *on time* (punctual), *in time* (early enough) or *just in the nick of time* (at the last possible moment).

L.e: The party went on into the early hours. Why do flights always leave at such ungodly hours? The farmers worked from dawn till dusk. We arrived just in the nick of time to catch the train.

L.p: Time can pass slowly or quickly: *time flies* when you're enjoying yourself, and *time drags* when you're bored. A *brief period* is short; *for the time being* means for now. Something that happens *once in a while* is occasional.

L.e: Time flies when you're on holiday. The last hour of the meeting really dragged. For the time being, I'm living with my parents. We eat out once in a while.

units.sub: break the silence, excessive noise, almighty bang

L.p: A place can be *completely silent* or in *total silence*. Someone may *break the silence* by speaking first, and a room can *fall silent* when something surprising happens. An *awkward silence* is uncomfortable; a *stunned silence* follows shocking news.

L.e: Nobody spoke until the youngest child broke the silence. The audience fell silent as the lights went down. There was an awkward silence after his joke. The verdict was met with stunned silence.

L.p: Noise can be *loud*, *deafening* or *excessive* (more than is acceptable); people *make a noise* or, more informally, *make a racket*. You *hear a noise*; a sudden, very loud one is *an almighty bang* (informal) or *a deafening crash*. Neighbours may *complain about the noise*.

L.e: The council received complaints about excessive noise from the bar. The children were making a terrible racket. We heard an almighty bang from the kitchen. The music at the concert was deafening.

L.x: Please don't *make so much noise* (not *do so much noise*) – the baby's asleep.

L.p: Bells *ring*, *chime* or *toll*; a door *creaks*; a phone *beeps*; a crowd *roars*. Voices can be *raised* (louder, often angry) or *hushed* (very quiet).

L.e: The church bells rang at midday. The old door creaked as it opened. The crowd roared when the team scored. They spoke in hushed voices in the library.

units.sub: within commuting distance, painfully thin, vast majority

L.p: A place can be *within walking distance* or *within commuting distance* (close enough to travel to work daily). Something *a short distance away* is near; something in *the far distance* is very far. A place *a stone's throw from* somewhere is very close. You *cover a distance* when you travel it.

L.e: We wanted a house within commuting distance of London. The station is a stone's throw from our flat. In the far distance we could see the mountains. The cyclists covered a distance of 160 kilometres.

L.p: Things can be *tiny*, *vast* or *huge*; *the vast majority* means almost all. People can be *painfully thin* (so thin that it's worrying). We talk about *a narrow margin* (a small difference), *a wide range* and *a broad smile*. A large group of something is *a sizeable number*.

L.e: The vast majority of students passed the exam. After his illness he was painfully thin. The team won by a narrow margin. The shop sells a wide range of cheeses. She greeted us with a broad smile.

L.x: The *vast majority* (not *the big majority*) of people agreed with the plan.

L.p: You can *take measurements*, *measure up* a room (for furniture), or describe things as *two metres high*, *ten metres long* and *five metres wide*. A thing that is *full-size* is not a small model.

L.e: The builder took measurements of the kitchen. The wall is three metres high and twelve metres long. They built a full-size copy of the ship.

units.sub: bright colour, beam of light, shed some light on

L.p: Colours can be *bright*, *vivid* or *bold*, or *pale*, *soft* and *pastel*. A colour that is too strong is *garish*. Colours *match* or *clash*; one colour can *fade* in the sun. We often add *light* or *dark* (*dark green*) or *-ish* (*greenish*).

L.e: Children's toys often come in bright colours. The bedroom is painted a soft blue. His orange tie clashed with his pink shirt. My favourite jeans have faded after years of washing.

L.x: I love *bright colours* (not *strong colours*) in summer clothes.

L.p: Light can be *bright*, *dim* or *soft*. A torch or lighthouse sends out a *beam of light*; the sun gives *a ray of sunshine*. Lights *flicker*, *flash* and *go out*. A room can be *brightly lit* or *poorly lit*.

L.e: A beam of light from the lighthouse swept across the sea. A ray of sunshine came through the curtains. The candles flickered in the wind. The corridor was poorly lit and slightly scary.

L.p: Light is used in many metaphorical collocations: to *shed some light on* something is to help explain it; to *come to light* is to become known; to *see the light* is to finally understand; and to *make light of* a problem is to treat it as less serious than it is.

L.e: New documents shed some light on the mystery. Further problems came to light during the inspection. He finally saw the light and apologised. She made light of her injury, but it was serious.

units.sub: choppy sea, soft pillow, ice melts

L.p: Surfaces can be *smooth*, *rough*, *bumpy*, *slippery* or *sticky*. Water has its own collocations: a *calm sea*, a *choppy sea* (with many small waves), *rough seas*, *still water*. A road can be *bumpy* or have a *smooth surface*.

L.e: The ferry crossing was uncomfortable because of the choppy sea. The lake was perfectly still in the morning. Be careful – the floor is slippery. The road through the village was very bumpy.

L.p: A *soft pillow*, *soft fur* and *soft skin* are pleasant to touch; *hard ground* and *stiff* new shoes are not. Bread can be *fresh* or *stale*; meat can be *tender* or *tough*; vegetables can be *crisp* or *soggy*.

L.e: I can't sleep without a soft pillow. The ground was too hard to dig. My new shoes are still a bit stiff. The steak was so tender it melted in your mouth. Nobody likes soggy chips.

L.x: This bread is *stale* (not *old*) – let's buy a fresh loaf.

L.p: Ice *melts* when it gets warm and water *freezes* when it gets cold; snow *thaws*. Butter *softens* at room temperature, chocolate can *melt* in your hand, and concrete *sets* (becomes hard).

L.e: The ice on the pond melted in the afternoon sun. The lake freezes every winter. Leave the butter out so it softens. Don't walk on the concrete until it has set.

units.sub: fragrant perfume, have a taste, smell danger

L.p: Before deciding whether you like a new dish, you might *have a taste* – try a small amount. Food can be *sweet*, *bitter*, *sour*, *salty* or *spicy*, with *a strong flavour* or *a mild flavour*. Food that is *tasteless* has hardly any flavour at all, and people who love sugary things *have a sweet tooth*.

L.e: Can I have a taste of your curry? This coffee has a bitter taste. The sauce has a mild flavour, so children like it. I have a terrible sweet tooth – I love cakes.

L.p: Pleasant smells: a *fragrant perfume*, the *aroma of* coffee, the *scent of* roses. Unpleasant smells: a *strong smell*, a *musty smell* (old and damp), the *stench of* rubbish. A smell can *fill the room* or *linger* (stay for a long time).

L.e: She wore a light, fragrant perfume. The aroma of fresh bread filled the kitchen. The old attic had a musty smell. The smell of smoke lingered for days.

L.x: The *smell of coffee* (not *the smelling of coffee*) woke me up.

L.p: Some smell collocations are figurative: animals – and people – can *smell danger*; you *smell a rat* when you suspect something is wrong; and you *catch a whiff of* something when you notice it briefly.

L.e: The deer smelled danger and ran into the trees. When he offered me such a cheap price, I smelled a rat. I caught a whiff of perfume as she walked past.

units.sub: significant number, come to a total of, rare species

L.p: *Number* goes with countable nouns and *amount* with uncountable ones: *a large number of* visitors, *a small amount of* sugar. Formal writing uses *a significant number*, *a considerable amount* and *a substantial sum*. When you add things up, they *come to a total of* a figure, and you can give *a rough estimate* or *an exact figure*.

L.e: A significant number of students work part-time. The repairs cost a considerable amount of money. The bill came to a total of £86. At a rough estimate, two hundred people attended.

L.x: There was *a large amount of* (not *a large number of*) traffic on the bridge.

L.p: Things happen *on a regular basis*, *from time to time*, *every now and then* or *once in a blue moon* (very rarely). A *rare species* is an animal or plant that is hard to find; a *common occurrence* happens often; an *isolated incident* happens only once.

L.e: The committee meets on a regular basis. We see each other from time to time. The tiger is a rare species in this region. Power cuts are a common occurrence here. Police say the attack was an isolated incident.

L.p: Numbers *rise steadily*, *increase sharply*, *double* or *treble*; they *fall dramatically* or *decline gradually*. A figure can *reach a peak* (its highest point) or *hit a record low*.

L.e: Visitor numbers have risen steadily since 2015. The price of tickets doubled in two years. Unemployment reached a peak in 2010. The number of bees has fallen dramatically.

units.sub: prompt payment, painfully slow, lose your balance

L.p: Things can happen *at great speed*, *at top speed* or *at a snail's pace*. A *prompt reply* or *prompt payment* comes quickly and on time. Progress can be *rapid*, or *painfully slow* (so slow that it's frustrating). A vehicle can *pick up speed* or *slow down*.

L.e: The ambulance raced along at top speed. Thank you for your prompt reply. Progress on the new bridge has been painfully slow. The train picked up speed as it left the station. Traffic moved at a snail's pace.

L.x: We would appreciate *prompt payment* (not *quick payment of the bill*) within ten days.

L.p: People and things *move freely*, *move slowly*, *change direction* or *come to a halt*. If you are unsteady, you may *lose your balance* and *fall over*; someone may *keep their balance* on a narrow path. A crowd *surges forward*; cars *move bumper to bumper* in heavy traffic.

L.e: The bus came to a sudden halt. I slipped on the ice and lost my balance. It's hard to keep your balance on a moving train. When the doors opened, the crowd surged forward.

L.p: Some verbs describe quick, sudden movements: you *jump to your feet*, *spring into action*, *swerve to avoid* something or *duck* to avoid being hit.

L.e: When the fire alarm rang, everyone jumped to their feet. The staff sprang into action when the guests arrived. The driver swerved to avoid a fox.

units.sub: make an adjustment, break a habit, change the subject

L.p: You *make a change*, *make an adjustment* (a small change to improve something) or *make alterations* (to clothes or buildings). Changes can be *minor*, *major*, *radical* or *gradual*. Organisations *bring about change* or *introduce changes*.

L.e: The mechanic made a small adjustment to the brakes. The tailor made some alterations to my jacket. The new manager introduced radical changes. Climate change is bringing about major changes in farming.

L.x: We need to *make a few adjustments* (not *do a few adjustments*) to the plan.

L.p: You *break a habit* or *kick a habit* (informal), *change your mind*, *change your plans* and *change the subject* when you start talking about something different. A *change of heart* is a change in your opinion or feelings; a *change of scene* is a new place that makes you feel better.

L.e: He broke the habit of checking his phone at dinner. I've changed my mind – I'll come with you. Every time I mention money, she changes the subject. After meeting the family, he had a change of heart. A week in the mountains was a welcome change of scene.

L.p: Prices, temperatures and moods *fluctuate* (keep changing). Things can *change dramatically*, *change for the better* or *change for the worse*. A situation that *transforms* changes completely.

L.e: Prices fluctuate from month to month. The neighbourhood has changed for the better since the new park opened. Her health changed dramatically after the operation.

units.sub: brief chat, raise a subject, drop a hint

L.p: You *have a chat* or *a brief chat* (a short, friendly talk); *strike up a conversation* (start one, often with a stranger); *have a heart-to-heart* (an honest, private talk); and *make small talk* (polite conversation about unimportant things). If two people talk at length, they *have a long talk*.

L.e: We had a brief chat in the corridor. I struck up a conversation with the woman next to me on the bus. My mother and I had a heart-to-heart about my future. I'm not very good at making small talk at parties.

L.p: In a meeting or conversation you *raise a subject* or *bring up a topic* (mention it for discussion), *get to the point* (talk about the important thing), *change the subject*, or *go off the subject*. If you *drop a hint*, you say something indirectly so that someone will guess what you mean.

L.e: Can I raise a subject that's been worrying me? He took ages to get to the point. Sorry, I've gone off the subject. She dropped a hint that she'd like a bike for her birthday.

L.x: I'll *raise the subject* (not *lift the subject*) at the next meeting.

L.p: People *speak their mind* (say what they really think), *put it bluntly* (say it directly), *choose their words carefully* and *keep their voice down*. If you *beat about the bush*, you avoid saying something directly.

L.e: My grandmother always speaks her mind. To put it bluntly, your plan won't work. The minister chose her words carefully. Please keep your voice down – the baby's sleeping. Stop beating about the bush and tell me what happened.

units.sub: pace up and down, wander aimlessly, faltering steps

L.p: English has many verbs for walking. You *stroll* along a beach (walk slowly for pleasure), *march* (walk with firm, regular steps), *stride* (walk with long steps), *tiptoe* (walk quietly on your toes), *stagger* (walk unsteadily) and *limp* (walk with difficulty because of an injury).

L.e: We strolled along the seafront after dinner. The soldiers marched through the square. She strode confidently into the room. I tiptoed past the baby's room. He staggered home after the party. After the match, the goalkeeper limped off the pitch.

L.p: Some walking verbs have typical partners: you *pace up and down* when you are nervous; you *wander aimlessly* without a plan; a toddler takes *faltering steps* (unsteady ones); you *retrace your steps* when you go back the way you came; and you *quicken your pace* when you walk faster.

L.e: He paced up and down the hospital corridor. We wandered aimlessly round the old town. The baby took her first faltering steps. I'd lost my keys, so I retraced my steps. When it started to rain, we quickened our pace.

L.x: I *retraced my steps* (not *repeated my steps*) to look for my phone.

L.p: People *go for a walk*, *take the dog for a walk*, *go hiking* or *go rambling*. A walk can be *brisk* (fast), *leisurely* (relaxed) or *bracing* (cold and refreshing).

L.e: Let's go for a walk before lunch. My dad takes the dog for a walk every morning. We went for a brisk walk along the cliffs. A bracing walk by the sea will wake you up.
