units.sub: promising start, bring something to an end, from scratch

L.p: Things can *get off to a good start* or *a promising start*, or *get off to a bad start*. You *make a start on* a task, *start from scratch* (from the very beginning, with nothing prepared) and *set the ball rolling* (start an activity that others will continue). Plans *get under way* when they begin.

L.e: The new café got off to a promising start. Let's make a start on the washing-up. The file was lost, so we had to start from scratch. I'll set the ball rolling by introducing myself. Building work finally got under way in March.

L.x: Let's *make a start* (not *do a start*) on the report this afternoon.

L.p: You *keep going*, *carry on* or *press on* with something despite difficulties; a situation *drags on* when it continues for too long. Work that *is in progress* has started but not finished.

L.e: We were tired, but we pressed on to the top. The dispute dragged on for months. The new library is still a work in progress.

L.p: You can *bring something to an end*, *come to an end*, *put an end to* something (stop it, especially something bad) or *draw to a close* (gradually end). Tasks are *completed*; meetings are *wound up*. If something ends suddenly, it *comes to an abrupt end*.

L.e: The president brought the meeting to an end at five. The government promised to put an end to child poverty. As the evening drew to a close, people started to leave. Their holiday came to an abrupt end when the flight was cancelled.

units.sub: make a breakthrough, fail miserably, against all odds

L.p: People *achieve success*, *make a breakthrough* (an important discovery or development), *reach their goals* and *pull something off* (succeed in doing something difficult). A plan that works perfectly is *a resounding success* or *a roaring success*. If you succeed despite huge difficulties, you succeed *against all odds*.

L.e: Scientists have made a breakthrough in the treatment of malaria. The charity concert was a resounding success. Nobody thought we could win, but we pulled it off. Against all odds, the small club won the cup.

L.p: Things can *fail miserably* (very badly), *fall through* (not happen, of plans), *go wrong* or *come to nothing*. Something that fails completely is *a complete failure* or *a total disaster*; a person might *fail an exam* or *fail to meet a deadline*.

L.e: Our attempt to bake a wedding cake failed miserably. The deal fell through at the last minute. All our efforts came to nothing. The opening night was a total disaster.

L.x: His plan *failed miserably* (not *failed sadly*) – nobody came.

L.p: You *make an attempt*, *do your utmost* (try as hard as possible), *give it a try* or *have a go*. If at first you fail, you might *try again* or *give up*. A *narrow defeat* is losing by a small amount.

L.e: She made a brave attempt to swim the channel. We'll do our utmost to help. It looks difficult, but give it a try. After three narrow defeats, the team finally won.

units.sub: cause alarm, adverse effects, have a major impact

L.p: Things *cause problems*, *cause damage*, *cause alarm* or *cause concern* (make people worried). Something can *lead to* a result, *give rise to* a situation or *trigger* a reaction (cause it to start suddenly). The *main cause* or *root cause* is the most basic reason.

L.e: The rumours caused alarm among parents. Heavy rain caused damage to the bridge. Poor diet can lead to heart disease. The decision triggered angry protests. Lack of money is the root cause of the problem.

L.p: Something *has an effect on* something else; effects can be *positive*, *negative*, *harmful*, *long-term* or *adverse* (bad, often in medical or official contexts). A big change *has a major impact on* people; a small one has a *minor impact*.

L.e: The medicine has no adverse effects for most patients. Social media has had a major impact on politics. The new law could have long-term effects on small businesses. The rain had little effect on the crowd.

L.x: The cuts will *have an effect on* (not *make an effect on*) local schools.

L.p: Actions *have consequences*; you *face the consequences* or *suffer the consequences* of your choices. As *a direct result of* something, another thing happens. Results can be *disastrous*, *far-reaching* (affecting many things) or *unexpected*.

L.e: If you break the rules, you'll have to face the consequences. As a direct result of the strike, flights were cancelled. The discovery had far-reaching consequences for medicine.

units.sub: vaguely remember, sense danger, jog your memory

L.p: You can *vaguely remember* something (not clearly), *distinctly remember* it (very clearly), or *remember* it *vividly*. Memories can be *happy*, *painful* or *fond* (warm and loving). Something can *bring back memories* or *jog your memory* (help you remember). If you completely forget, your *mind goes blank*.

L.e: I vaguely remember meeting him at a wedding. I distinctly remember locking the door. That song brings back happy memories of university. This photo might jog your memory. In the exam my mind went blank.

L.x: I *vaguely remember* (not *lightly remember*) the house where I was born.

L.p: You *completely forget*, *forget all about* something, or have *a memory like a sieve* (forget things easily). A name can be *on the tip of your tongue* (you almost remember it). Things *slip your mind* when you forget to do them.

L.e: I completely forgot about your birthday – I'm so sorry. His name is on the tip of my tongue. It slipped my mind to call the dentist. I've got a memory like a sieve.

L.p: Our senses warn us about the world around us. Animals and people *sense danger* or *sense a change* in the air, and sometimes you just *have a feeling* that all is not well. To *catch sight of* something is to see it for a moment, often by chance, and a *gut feeling* is an instinct you trust without being able to explain it.

L.e: The birds sensed danger and flew away. I had a feeling that something was wrong. I caught sight of her in the crowd. My gut feeling is that he's lying.

units.sub: reach a consensus, beg to differ, see eye to eye

L.p: You can *agree wholeheartedly* (completely), *broadly agree* (agree with the main points), or *be in complete agreement*. Groups *reach a consensus* (a general agreement) or *reach an agreement*. People who agree *see eye to eye*.

L.e: I agree wholeheartedly with what you said. We broadly agree, but we have a few concerns. After a long debate, the committee reached a consensus. My sister and I rarely see eye to eye about politics.

L.x: The committee finally *reached a consensus* (not *got a consensus*) on the budget.

L.p: Polite ways to disagree include *beg to differ* (formal), *take a different view* and *have reservations* (some doubts). Stronger: *strongly disagree*, *totally disagree*. When people accept that they disagree, they *agree to differ*. A *difference of opinion* is a disagreement.

L.e: I beg to differ – I think the old system was better. The report takes a different view. I have reservations about the cost. Let's agree to differ and move on. There was a difference of opinion about the route.

L.p: Disagreements can turn into *a heated argument* or *a bitter dispute*; people *settle* or *resolve* a dispute; they *find common ground* (discover areas of agreement) or *meet halfway* (each give something).

L.e: The neighbours had a bitter dispute about the fence. The two sides finally resolved the dispute. We found common ground on most issues. Let's meet halfway – I'll pay for dinner if you pay for the taxi.

units.sub: firmly believe, hold strong views, change your mind

L.p: You can *firmly believe*, *strongly believe* or *genuinely believe* something; you *have faith in* a person or idea, and *put your trust in* someone. A *deeply held belief* is very important to someone. A *popular belief* is held by many people, but may be wrong.

L.e: I firmly believe that education should be free. She has great faith in her doctors. These are deeply held beliefs that are hard to change. Contrary to popular belief, bats are not blind.

L.x: I *firmly believe* (not *heavily believe*) that we can win.

L.p: People *hold strong views* or *have strong opinions* on topics; they *express a view*, *voice an opinion* and *share a view*. An opinion can be *personal*, *honest* or *considered* (carefully thought about). In discussions, you might *keep an open mind* (be willing to consider new ideas).

L.e: My grandfather holds strong views on politics. Several parents voiced their opinions at the meeting. In my honest opinion, the film was too long. It's important to keep an open mind about new ideas.

L.p: You *change your mind*, *have second thoughts* (begin to doubt a decision), *come round to* an idea (start to accept it) or *see things differently*. If you *stick to your guns*, you refuse to change your opinion.

L.e: I was going to buy the car, but I had second thoughts. At first Dad hated the idea of a dog, but he's come round to it. Despite the criticism, she stuck to her guns.

units.sub: make a choice, take a decision, weigh up the options

L.p: You *make a decision* or *take a decision* (both are used in British English); decisions can be *difficult*, *final*, *hasty* (too quick) or *unanimous* (everyone agrees). You *reach a decision* after discussion and *stand by your decision* (not change it). You can also *make up your mind*.

L.e: We took the decision to move to the coast. It was a hasty decision, and we regretted it. The jury's decision was unanimous. I can't make up my mind about the job. She stood by her decision despite the criticism.

L.p: You *make a choice*, *have a choice*, *have no choice but to* do something, and *be spoilt for choice* (have too many options). Before choosing, you *weigh up the options* or *consider the alternatives*; an option can be *the best option*, *the only option* or *the last resort*.

L.e: We had no choice but to cancel the trip. In the bakery we were spoilt for choice. Let's weigh up the options before we decide. Borrowing money should be the last resort.

L.x: She *made a choice* (not *did a choice*) between the two universities.

L.p: When you can't decide, you are *in two minds* about something, or you *sit on the fence* (avoid taking a side). You might want to *sleep on it* (decide the next day) or *toss a coin*.

L.e: I'm in two minds about selling the house. Politicians often sit on the fence. Don't decide now – sleep on it. We couldn't agree, so we tossed a coin.

units.sub: make a claim, flatly deny, admit defeat

L.p: To *make a claim* is to say that something is true when other people may doubt it. A claim can be *bold*, *wild* (made without much thought), *false*, *exaggerated* or *unfounded* (with no facts behind it). You *back up a claim* or *support a claim* with evidence, while others may *dispute a claim*, *dismiss a claim* or *reject a claim*. A group can *claim responsibility for* an attack. When you ask an insurance company for money, you *put in a claim*.

L.e: The company made some wild claims about its new phone. Can you back up that claim with figures? The minister dismissed the claims as nonsense. No group has yet claimed responsibility for the explosion. After the flood we put in a claim for the ruined carpets.

L.x: They *made a claim* (not *did a claim*) on their travel insurance.

L.p: When you say firmly that something is not true, you *deny* it. You can *flatly deny*, *strongly deny*, *categorically deny* or *vehemently deny* it – all of these mean very firmly. People *deny an allegation*, *deny a rumour* or *deny any wrongdoing*; someone who says they know nothing about a matter *denies all knowledge of* it. An organisation can *issue a denial*. *There's no denying* that something is true means that everyone has to accept it.

L.e: The player flatly denied taking money from the club. A spokesperson categorically denied the rumours of a merger. The manager denied all knowledge of the missing files. The palace issued a denial within the hour. There's no denying that the new bridge has made life easier.

L.x: She *denied* (not *refused*) that she had opened the letter.

L.p: The opposite of denying is admitting. You can *freely admit* or *readily admit* something (without hesitating), or *grudgingly admit* it (unwillingly). When you accept that you cannot win, you *admit defeat*, and a company *admits liability* when it accepts legal responsibility. When you say that someone has done wrong, you *make an accusation* or *make an allegation*; allegations can be *serious* or *unfounded*, and people *face allegations* or *face accusations*.

L.e: I freely admit that I know nothing about cars. He grudgingly admitted that his sister had been right. After three hours of trying, we admitted defeat and called a taxi. The insurers refused to admit liability. A local paper made serious allegations about the mayor. The coach now faces accusations of bullying.

units.sub: take a liking to, can't stand, have a soft spot for

L.p: When you start to like someone or something, you *take a liking to* them; if it happens quickly, often with something you would like to own, you *take a fancy to* it (informal). If you *have a soft spot for* someone, you feel affection for them even though they are not perfect. You can be *very fond of*, *really keen on* or *a big fan of* something, and you *thoroughly enjoy* the things you like a lot. Something that *grows on you* is something you come to like little by little.

L.e: Our cat has taken a liking to the new neighbour. My mum took a fancy to a red coat in a shop window. I've always had a soft spot for old cars. I'm not very keen on horror films. We thoroughly enjoyed the concert. I didn't like the song at first, but it's grown on me.

L.x: She *thoroughly enjoyed* (not *strongly enjoyed*) her holiday in Wales.

L.p: The strongest everyday ways to show dislike are *can't stand*, *can't bear* and *loathe*; you can also *detest* something. If you dislike someone from the moment you meet them, you *take an instant dislike to* them. A *pet hate* (in American English, a *pet peeve*) is a small thing that annoys you a lot. If you *go off* something, you stop liking it, and if something *isn't your cup of tea*, it isn't the kind of thing you enjoy. If you *have no time for* someone, you neither respect them nor want their company.

L.e: I can't stand people who talk during films. She can't bear the sound of chalk on a board. The children took an instant dislike to their new babysitter. My pet hate is people who never answer messages. I went off coffee when I was ill. Opera isn't really my cup of tea. I have no time for people who are rude to waiters.

L.x: I *can't stand* (not *can't support*) loud music in restaurants.

L.p: You *have a preference for* the thing you like more than the others, and a *strong preference* is a clear one. *Given the choice*, you would pick one thing over another, and you *would rather* do one thing than another. Likes and dislikes that are personal are *a matter of taste*, and something you need time to learn to like is *an acquired taste*.

L.e: Most guests had a strong preference for the vegetarian menu. Given the choice, I'd live by the sea. I'd rather walk than wait for the bus. Whether you like modern art is a matter of taste. Olives are an acquired taste.

units.sub: pay tribute to, come under fire, constructive criticism

L.p: To praise someone formally, for example at a ceremony or after their death, you *pay tribute to* them. Praise can be *high*, *warm* or *lavish* (a great deal of it); you *heap praise on* someone when you praise them a lot, and you *sing someone's praises* when you tell everybody how good they are. People *win praise* or *earn praise* for what they do. You *pay someone a compliment* or *compliment someone on* something, and you *give credit where credit is due* when you praise someone who deserves it. A show that critics love *gets rave reviews*.

L.e: The prime minister paid tribute to the firefighters. The critics heaped praise on her first novel. Our neighbours are always singing the praises of their builder. The nurses won praise for their calm response. He complimented me on my cooking. The play got rave reviews in every paper.

L.x: She *paid me a compliment* (not *made me a compliment*) about my presentation.

L.p: When people start to criticise someone in public, that person *comes under fire* or *comes in for criticism*. Criticism can be *fierce*, *harsh*, *severe* or *scathing* (very strong and unkind); if it helps the person to improve, it is *constructive criticism*. Decisions *attract criticism* or *draw criticism*, and people *face criticism*. You can be *highly critical of* something, *find fault with* it (look for things that are wrong) or *pick holes in* it (find the weak points in an argument or plan).

L.e: The government has come under fire for raising fares again. The referee came in for some harsh criticism after the match. Good teachers give constructive criticism. The new logo drew criticism from fans. The report was highly critical of the hospital. My father finds fault with everything I cook. The lawyer picked holes in the witness's story.

L.x: The film received *harsh criticism* (not *hard criticism*) from reviewers.

L.h: C Reacting to praise and criticism

L.p: Some people *take criticism well*; others *take it badly* or *take it personally*. You can *respond to criticism*, *defend yourself against criticism* or simply *brush off criticism* (treat it as unimportant). If someone says something that sounds critical but you choose to hear it as praise, you *take it as a compliment*. A small piece of praise for something you did well is *a pat on the back*.

L.e: He's never been good at taking criticism. Try not to take it personally – she's like that with everyone. The coach brushed off the criticism and focused on the next game. 'You're very stubborn.' 'I'll take that as a compliment!' The whole team deserve a pat on the back.

units.sub: lasting happiness, worried sick, emotional wreck

L.p: Happiness can be *lasting* (it continues for a long time), *true* or *perfect*, and joy or delight can be *sheer* or *pure* (complete, with nothing else mixed in). When you are extremely happy, you *jump for joy*, or – informally – you are *over the moon* or *on cloud nine*. When a worry ends, you *feel a sense of relief* and *breathe a sigh of relief*. Doing something difficult well gives you *a sense of achievement* or *great satisfaction*.

L.e: Money doesn't always bring lasting happiness. The children shrieked with sheer delight. She was over the moon when she got into medical school. We breathed a sigh of relief when the plane landed safely. Finishing the marathon gave him a real sense of achievement.

L.x: We *breathed a sigh of relief* (not *took a sigh of relief*) when the results came out.

L.p: If you are *worried sick*, you are extremely worried. People can be *deeply upset*, *bitterly disappointed* or *desperately unhappy*. You *burst into tears* when you suddenly start to cry, you are *close to tears* when you nearly cry, and you are *in floods of tears* when you cry a great deal. *A lump in your throat* is the tight feeling you get when you are moved and about to cry. If you *feel down* or *feel low*, you are a little sad.

L.e: Where have you been? We've been worried sick! The fans were bitterly disappointed by the result. When she heard the news, she burst into tears. By the end of the wedding speech, half the guests were close to tears. I've been feeling a bit down since the holidays ended.

L.x: I was *bitterly disappointed* (not *strongly disappointed*) with my mark.

L.p: After a very stressful time, you might be *an emotional wreck* – unable to control your feelings. If you have *mixed feelings* about something, you are partly happy and partly unhappy about it. You can *hurt someone's feelings*, *show your feelings* or *hide your feelings*; if you never let them out, you *bottle up your feelings*. When people disagree strongly, *feelings run high*. You can *lose your temper* or *keep your temper*, and you can be *overcome with emotion* – so moved that you can't speak or act normally.

L.e: After the funeral I was an emotional wreck. I have mixed feelings about leaving home. I didn't mean to hurt your feelings. It isn't healthy to bottle up your feelings. Feelings ran high at the meeting about the new road. He lost his temper and shouted at the referee. Accepting the prize, she was overcome with emotion.

units.sub: forward a message, email bounces, a computer crashes

L.p: You *send an email*, *reply to* it, or *forward a message* (send it on to someone else). You *attach a file* to an email, and the person who receives it *opens the attachment*. If an address is wrong, the email *bounces* – it comes back to you. Unwanted emails are *junk mail* or *spam*, and many of them end up in your *spam folder*. When too many messages arrive, your *inbox fills up*. You *copy someone in* (or *cc* them) when you want them to see a message as well.

L.e: Could you forward me the message from the landlord? I've attached the photos to this email. Don't open an attachment from someone you don't know. My email bounced – I must have typed the address wrongly. Your reply went into my spam folder. Please copy me in on any emails to the client.

L.x: I *sent you an email* (not *wrote you a mail*) yesterday.

L.p: You *switch on* or *start up* a computer, *log in* or *log on* with your *username* and *password*, and *log out* or *log off* when you have finished. You *save a file*, *back up* your files (make copies in case something goes wrong), *download* or *install* software, and *upgrade to* a newer version. To find information, you *go online*, *browse the web*, *click on a link* and *type in a search term*.

L.e: Always back up your files before you install an update. I can't log in – I think I've forgotten my password. Click on the link at the bottom of the page. The app is free to download. Remember to save the file before you close it.

L.p: A computer can *crash* (stop working completely) or *freeze* (stop responding), and then you have to *restart* or *reboot* it. If you hadn't saved your work, you may *lose data*. A file can *become corrupted* – damaged so that it can't be opened. A *virus* can *infect* a computer, and criminals *hack into* systems. Sometimes *the connection drops*, *a website goes down* or a device *runs out of memory*.

L.e: My laptop crashed and I lost two hours of work. The screen has frozen again – try restarting it. The file is corrupted, so I can't open it. Someone hacked into the school's system. The bank's website went down for most of the morning. The connection keeps dropping in the kitchen.
